conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I really will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doc. I’ll take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Call your doctor in a week, and go to the ER if you have chest pain, vomiting blood, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No alcohol, take my meds, and follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You did well this time. Let’s keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, I’m Dr. Reyes. You’re in the hospital because you came in with chest pain after being punched near your defibrillator. We’re going to figure out what’s going on. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hurting here, right over the device. It’s tender when I move or breathe deep. And I’ve been nauseous, throwing up a few times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned the device fired four times? We checked with electrophysiology, and the device didn’t actually fire. There’s no record of shocks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, really? I felt something—like jolts. But maybe it was just the punch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The trauma could definitely cause that sensation. We did a chest X-ray, and there’s no fracture or damage to the device. Your heart rhythm is irregular, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… but I also have pain in my upper right belly and I’ve been dizzy for about two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. You had a fall recently with a head strike? Your CT head was normal, so we’re not worried about a brain injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I slipped. But the dizziness hasn’t gone away. And the headaches are bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those could be related to alcohol withdrawal. Your blood alcohol level was very high—323—when you arrived. That’s severe intoxication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had two pints earlier that day. But I didn’t think it was that bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, especially with your heart condition. We’re monitoring you for withdrawal symptoms. We’ve started you on vitamins and a medication called diazepam to help prevent seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been shaky and sweating. Is that part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are classic signs. We’re scoring your symptoms regularly. You’ve needed a few doses because you scored high on the scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay? I don’t want to have a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not showing signs of serious withdrawal so far. No hallucinations or confusion. We’re giving you medication to keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve got some test results. Your liver enzymes are elevated—AST is higher than ALT—which suggests recent heavy drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean my liver is damaged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely alcohol-induced injury, but not permanent if you stop drinking. Your ultrasound showed no gallstones or liver disease. We also saw some old rib fractures on the X-ray—probably from past trauma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember breaking ribs. But I’ve had rough times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re healing. But back to your belly pain and nausea—we think it’s from alcohol use and gastritis. We’ve increased your omeprazole and added anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Last time, I was putting food in my vomit bin. I was confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was noted in your last admission. We’re watching closely. Your heart function is still weak—EF around 25%—but stable. No signs of heart failure worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your heart enzymes twice—both negative. No heart attack. EKG shows old damage but no new changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But I took eight nitroglycerin pills. Was that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. It can cause headaches and low blood pressure. But it didn’t help, which makes us think the pain isn’t from heart ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the chest pain is just from the punch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. There’s tenderness over the device pocket, but no infection or fluid collection. We’ll keep it clean and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show low potassium and magnesium. That’s common with vomiting and your diuretic. We’re giving supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take potassium at home. But I haven’t been regular with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We repleted it. You also had a short run of fast heartbeats on the monitor—8 beats—but it stopped on its own. Likely due to low electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It was brief and asymptomatic. We’re correcting the levels to prevent more episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bilirubin is high—mostly indirect. But ultrasound is normal, and you’re not anemic. This looks like Gilbert’s syndrome, which you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not liver failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. It’s a mild genetic condition. It can flare with fasting or illness, like now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight. Your tremors are gone, and you haven’t vomited. We’re stopping the withdrawal meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. What about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning discharge today. Continue all your heart meds—especially dabigatran for stroke prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should improve. Use acetaminophen if needed. Avoid alcohol completely—it’s dangerous with your heart and liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need to stop. It’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can connect you with support services. Your health depends on it. Also, weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Stay safe and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, I’m Dr. Reyes. You’re in the hospital after being punched in the chest. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I had a few drinks, got into a fight over money. Guy hit me right here—on my chest. Felt a shock right after. Thought my defibrillator went off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We checked your device, and it didn’t fire. No shocks were delivered. Your heart rhythm was fast, but not dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I felt it. I know I did. It zapped me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes the sensation of a punch near the device can feel like a shock. We’ve seen this before. The device logs show no therapy was given.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… okay. But my chest still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you pain medicine earlier, and your chest pain improved. We also did a CT scan to check for blood clots in your lungs. It came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No clots? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. Your heart enzymes were normal too—no sign of a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why was my heart racing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate was 140 when you arrived. That’s sinus tachycardia—your body’s response to stress, alcohol, and possibly withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking a lot lately. A pint yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your alcohol level was high—313. That’s severe intoxication. We’re treating you for withdrawal with diazepam to prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had withdrawal before. Shakes, nausea… it’s rough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring you closely. You’re getting vitamins—thiamine, folic acid—because alcohol depletes them. We don’t want any neurological issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My stomach’s been bothering me too. And my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had tenderness in your upper right abdomen and lower back. Your lipase was slightly elevated—could be mild pancreas irritation from alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had belly pain for months. Nausea too. Even when I’m not drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s chronic. We think it’s related to gastritis or maybe ongoing liver issues. But it’s not an emergency now. You’re tolerating liquids okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I had some broth. Rice later. That usually helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on a BRAT diet—bananas, rice, applesauce, toast—for now. Advance as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, your liver enzymes were high when you came in—AST 126, ALT 51. That’s from alcohol. They’re improving now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My liver’s been messed up before. I know I need to stop drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stopping is the best thing for your heart and liver. Your cardiomyopathy—weak heart—is likely from long-term alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart’s only pumping at 16%? That’s bad, huh?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s reduced, yes. But it’s stable now. You’re on medications to protect it—metoprolol, losartan, furosemide. We’re increasing your metoprolol to 75mg daily to better control your heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I take that one every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate’s down to 110 now. That’s better. We gave you some metoprolol earlier. Still feeling anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little shaky. Nauseous again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you some promethazine for nausea. And another dose of diazepam. Your withdrawal symptoms should ease over the next day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your lipase is back to normal. Liver enzymes are improving too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my pancreas is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of acute pancreatitis. The elevation was likely due to dehydration and alcohol. We’re keeping you on fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been vomiting for months. Could that be something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It might be related to chronic gastritis or even mild opioid withdrawal—you mentioned using street oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, sometimes. Just to feel normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could contribute to nausea. We’re giving anti-nausea meds now, but long-term, you’ll need to stop all substances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Heart rate is 95, normal rhythm. No chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, feels fine. I’ve been thinking… I want help. For drinking. For everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. We can arrange rehab through the clinic. They’ll provide medical and behavioral support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need it. I can’t keep living like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your withdrawal symptoms have resolved. You didn’t need diazepam last night. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still tired, but no shakes, no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow to an extended care facility for rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to start fresh.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, you’re cleared for discharge. You’ll go to the rehab clinic today. Any questions before we go over instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—what meds am I taking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, plus three new ones: a multivitamin, folic acid, and thiamine—daily. Also, metoprolol is now 75mg once a day. And promethazine for nausea if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with Dr. Lin in cardiology on the 20th at 10:20 a.m. Keep weighing yourself daily—call if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. For everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay strong. This is your chance to turn things around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand the rehab will help with both alcohol and your overall health?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m ready to do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all your records. They’ll continue your cardiac care and support your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment with my primary doctor too, for the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re taking charge of your health. We’re proud of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. They’ll take you to the facility. Remember—no alcohol, take your meds, and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got it. This time, I’m not leaving AMA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Meléndez. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you to the van. We’ll follow up with the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I intend to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, I’m Dr. Reyes. You came in today because you were vomiting blood and had abdominal pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I woke up with bad stomach pain. Started throwing up, and there was blood. A lot of it. Felt dizzy, shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any black or tarry stools? Or blood in your bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just the blood when I threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And how much alcohol have you been drinking lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I drink about a pint of vodka every day. Have for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. We ran a test and your alcohol level is high—283. That’s significant. We’re concerned about your stomach bleeding, especially with your history of gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had an endoscopy before, right? They said I had gastritis and duodenitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. So this could be a flare-up, or possibly a small tear in your esophagus from vomiting. We’re giving you a medication called pantoprazole through your IV to help protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your blood count is stable, and you haven’t vomited blood since you got here. We’ll watch you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had chest pain earlier. Is my heart okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG and your troponin levels—both were normal. So no sign of a heart attack. Your chest pain may be related to the stress or from acid reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had heart problems before—weak heart, AFib, and that defibrillator.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. Your defibrillator is still in place and working. We’re monitoring your rhythm. You’re in AFib now, but your rate is okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been taking my heart meds. Ran out—furosemide, metoprolol, losartan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve restarted your metoprolol and losartan. We’re not restarting the furosemide because you’re not swollen or fluid overloaded right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my blood thinner? I take Pradaxa.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched you to a heparin drip while you’re here for safety, but we’ll switch you back to Pradaxa before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I feel better already. The pain’s not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’re also giving you fluids and medications for nausea. We did a CT scan to check your abdomen because your lactate level was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lactate? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sign of stress on the body. It was elevated, so we were worried about poor blood flow to your intestines. But the CT scan showed everything is fine—your blood vessels are open, no blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, no surgery needed. Your liver shows fatty changes, but that’s common with alcohol use. Nothing urgent there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I should stop drinking. But it’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins to help with that. And we’re watching you for withdrawal, but so far, you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Meléndez. Your lactate level has dropped to normal—1.5. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It means your body is recovering. Your liver enzymes were a bit high yesterday but are improving. We’ll keep you on the IV pantoprazole for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids today—water, broth. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on liquids yesterday. How’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No nausea. Can I have real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on a soft diet—applesauce, toast, maybe some chicken. We’ll watch you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. No further bleeding. We’re switching you from IV pantoprazole to oral omeprazole 40 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same thing, just by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It will help prevent stomach irritation and reduce acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on metoprolol, losartan, aspirin, and simvastatin. And we’ve restarted Pradaxa this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been here five days. You’re eating well, no pain, no bleeding. We’d like to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A social worker spoke with you—they tried to get you into rehab, but no beds were available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I wasn’t ready then. But they said a bed might open up tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The facility called—they may have a spot. The social worker will help you get there if you want.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’d like that. I need to stop drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. We’ll give you all your prescriptions today—heart meds, Pradaxa, omeprazole, vitamins. Please follow up with your doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are stable. You’re cleared to go home. Or, if you choose, to the rehab facility tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to go to rehab. I’ll call them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. The social worker will help you arrange it. You’ve made real progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel better than I have in a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself. And call the helpline if you ever need support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your prescriptions to the pharmacy. Your PCP will need to check your blood pressure and labs in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing. We’re proud of you. Take care, Mr. Meléndez.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—avoid alcohol completely. It’s hurting your liver and stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’m ready to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best news I’ve heard all day. Let’s get you discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, I'm Dr. Reyes. You're in the ICU because of your symptoms after the assault and because we're managing your alcohol withdrawal. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay, I guess. My chest hurts where I got punched, near the defibrillator. And I’ve been throwing up a little blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve checked your defibrillator with a chest X-ray, and it looks intact. No damage. The vomiting — was it coffee-ground-like or bright red?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Kind of brownish, like coffee grounds. Happened a couple times. I also coughed up a little blood, maybe from my nose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. We’ll keep an eye on it. You’ve been through withdrawal before, right? We’re giving you diazepam to help with the shakes and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had bad withdrawals. Seizures once. I haven’t had a drink in a day. I used to drink a pint of vodka daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That explains the high withdrawal risk. We’re monitoring your symptoms closely. Your labs show a slightly elevated lactate, but no infection. It’s likely from the withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? The lactate thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in this case. It’s elevated but stable, and we don’t see signs of organ damage. It should come down as you stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your lactate dropped to 1.2 this morning — that’s a good sign. Your heart enzymes are normal, so no heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My chest still hurts, but not as bad. I had a stabbing pain last night that woke me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that on the monitor. Your ECG showed some changes, but they’ve been seen before in old records. Not new heart damage. Pain improved with oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it helped. But nitro didn’t do anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That supports it being musculoskeletal — from the punch — not heart-related. We’ll keep managing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving you to the regular floor today. Your withdrawal symptoms are improving, and you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I threw up again last night — just food, no blood. But I still feel a little sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with withdrawal. We’re keeping you on IV fluids and a proton pump inhibitor for your stomach. We think the blood was from a small tear or gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time I was here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very similar. Your hemoglobin is stable, so no active bleeding. We’ll switch you to oral meds soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray was clear — no blockage. That’s good. You’re tolerating food well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I ate toast and soup. No vomiting since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep advancing your diet. Your heart rhythm is stable, and telemetry shows no dangerous arrhythmias.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t passed out again. But I did get shocked four times in the past month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your defibrillator records — no shocks were delivered here, and no abnormal rhythms. The shocks before may have been for fast rhythms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat ECGs are stable. The T-wave changes are chronic. No new heart damage. Your chest pain is much better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, only hurts when I press on it. I’ve been walking around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. You’re euvolemic — not fluid overloaded — so we’re continuing your heart meds: metoprolol, losartan, and we restarted Pradaxa.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to take those for a week — someone stole my pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. That’s risky with atrial fibrillation. We’re glad we could restart it safely now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cough is still there? CXR was clear — no pneumonia. Probably bronchitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, just a dry cough. Not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it in mind. No fever or shortness of breath, so likely mild.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a formal check of your defibrillator today — it’s working perfectly. No issues detected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried after getting punched there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. But the device is fine. Your face is bruised too — but no fracture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I got hit in the face too. It’s sore but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all stays well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? I don’t have any meds there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you prescriptions for everything — heart meds, PPI, vitamins. Social work tried to get you into rehab, but no beds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I wanted to go. I know I need to stop drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you find a program. For now, please take your meds and avoid alcohol. It’s hard on your heart and stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. You’re walking well, eating, no chest pain with activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I still don’t feel like taking the pills with me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but they’re important. Pradaxa prevents strokes, the PPI helps your stomach, and the others protect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Can I at least get the paperwork later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can, but please keep the prescriptions. If your weight goes up more than 3 pounds, call your doctor — could be heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No drinking, take meds, watch weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And follow up with cardiology and your primary doctor. You’ve done well this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for taking care of me. I’ll try to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. Take care, Mr. Meléndez.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One thing — the blood I coughed up. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely from a nosebleed, especially with dry air or irritation. But if you cough up more blood, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And if you feel dizzy or pass out, get checked immediately. Your defibrillator is working, but we want to prevent issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re strong, but your heart is weak. Medications and sobriety are your best protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Nurse will bring your discharge instructions and prescriptions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ll take them. Maybe this time I’ll use them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That would be a great step. Take care, Mr. Meléndez.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe and take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check in with your follow-up team to make sure they know you’re out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, I’m Dr. Reyes. You’re in the hospital because you passed out twice and said you vomited blood. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I just got out of the hospital yesterday. I went to church, had lunch, then when I left, I felt dizzy and passed out. My defibrillator went off—I felt the shock.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And then what happened after you passed out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I got up, went back inside, was confused for a bit. Then I threw up blood—dark red, like half a cup. I was still dizzy. Later, walking to the bridge, I passed out again. Felt another shock.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, stabbing pain yesterday. And it still hurts here”—points to left chest—“especially when I press. That’s where my ICD is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check that. Right now, you’re on a heart monitor. We did an ECG, and it shows your heart rhythm is normal—sinus rhythm. No signs of a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I *felt* the shocks. Why wouldn’t it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your defibrillator’s records. It didn’t deliver any shocks. Sometimes people feel a sensation that mimics a shock, but the device didn’t fire.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That doesn’t make sense. I *felt* it. Twice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But the device data is clear. We also monitored you overnight—only one short, five-beat run of fast rhythm, but you didn’t feel it. It’s not dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why did I pass out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure. Your blood pressure was stable when you stood up—no drop. Your labs are normal, including your red blood cell count—no sign of major bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I *did* vomit blood. I know what I saw.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool. One note says it was positive for blood, another says negative. But your hemoglobin hasn’t dropped. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you don’t believe me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you felt something. But we have to go by the tests. Given your history of gastritis and alcohol use, you might have mild bleeding, but not enough to require an endoscopy now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking much since last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed opiates and benzodiazepines, but no cocaine or alcohol. We couldn’t check your blood alcohol level after the fact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took some pain meds, yeah. But no alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re keeping you on the proton pump inhibitor for your stomach. And we restarted your blood thinner—Pradaxa—since your bleeding risk seems low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to eat. I’ve been NPO since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can start you on a light diet. But slowly—just water and crackers for now. We’ll advance if you keep it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs are stable. Hemoglobin still 10.4. No signs of internal bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? Any more episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Still no shocks from your ICD. Cardiology reviewed your case—they don’t think you need another device check now. Just follow up in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I *felt* it. How can they say it didn’t happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The device logs are very accurate. It didn’t fire. Sometimes anxiety or dizziness can feel like a shock. We’ll keep monitoring, but it’s likely not dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT head results—no bleeding, no stroke. Chest X-ray shows an enlarged heart, but no pneumonia or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the dizziness and passing out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have a clear answer. It could be a brief heart rhythm issue, but we didn’t catch it. Or it could be related to blood pressure, dehydration, or even anxiety. With no repeat episodes here, we think you’re safe to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re a bit anemic—hemoglobin is low but stable. That could contribute. But you’re walking fine, no falls. We think you’re strong enough to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays well. You’ll need to follow up with your cardiologist and primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have a place to stay. I sleep under the bridge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Social work spoke with you yesterday. They’re helping connect you with shelters and support services. It’s important you have a safe place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel better. I’m tired of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Stopping alcohol, taking your medications, and following up can help. We’re giving you prescriptions—especially the omeprazole for your stomach and your heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your H. pylori test is still pending, but everything else looks stable. We’re discharging you now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. If you vomit blood again or pass out, come back. But only if there’s clear evidence—like actual blood or injury. Otherwise, follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take this discharge sheet. Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds in a day, call your doctor—could be heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still likely from the recent trauma or your device. But if it gets worse or you have shortness of breath, get checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. And please, no alcohol. It’s making everything worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I really will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. Here’s your prescription for omeprazole—take it twice a day. And this number for the device clinic—call them this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe, Mr. Meléndez. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—don’t stop your Pradaxa. It prevents strokes. Even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You’re cleared to leave. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in clinic. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your meds, stay hydrated, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, I’m Dr. Reyes. You’re in the hospital after being found in an alley earlier tonight. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I got into a fight this morning. Some guy punched me right where my defibrillator is, stole my meds. I’ve had chest pain ever since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And when was the last time you drank?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: This morning, around 10. I had about a pint and a half of vodka. I was trying to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The paramedics said your blood sugar was low when they found you. They gave you glucose and juice, and it came up. We also checked your alcohol level—it’s high, 332.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I drink too much. But the chest pain’s real. It’s worse since the punch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re taking that seriously. You have a history of heart problems—weak heart muscle, atrial fibrillation, and that defibrillator for dangerous rhythms. So we need to rule out a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had chest pain for years. But this feels different. Sharp, constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an EKG and two troponin tests—those check for heart damage. Both were negative. Your EKG looks like your old ones, no new changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t look like a heart attack. We also did a chest X-ray. No fractures, no lung issues. Your device lead is in the right place, unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can you give me something for the pain? And my meds—I need my Pradaxa, my metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you aspirin and a dose of morphine for pain. We’ll restart your home meds—Pradaxa, metoprolol, losartan, the rest—as soon as we’re sure you’re not at risk for bleeding or low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my oxycodone? The pain’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you your usual 5 mg dose now. But we’re watching for signs of withdrawal—you’ve had seizures before when stopping alcohol suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I get shaky, nauseous. Once I had a seizure on the street.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using the CIWA scale to monitor you—checking your tremors, nausea, anxiety. We gave you diazepam earlier and will continue as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any nausea or shakes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little shaky. Headache. But no vomiting. Chest pain’s still there, dull now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Liver enzymes are slightly elevated, but no sign of pancreatitis. Your hemoglobin is stable, no anemia. We’re continuing your thiamine, folate, and multivitamins—important for your liver and nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking for years. I know it’s bad. But I don’t have anywhere to go, no support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Social work tried to talk to you yesterday. They can help connect you with shelters or detox programs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been to those places. They kick you out if you relapse. I just need my meds and to get back on my feet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve ruled out a heart attack, bleeding, and infection. Your chest pain is likely related to muscle trauma from the punch or your chronic condition. We’ll keep managing your withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay to leave? I feel fine, just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to keep you one more night to make sure withdrawal doesn’t worsen. You’ve had delirium tremens before—that’s dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. I need to get back. My stuff’s out there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made it through the night without seizures or severe withdrawal. That’s good. But your pain and symptoms don’t match up with the tests—we’re not seeing new heart damage or internal injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I told you what happened. I got punched. I need my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you’re in pain. But given your history—similar visits, symptoms not matching test results—we’re concerned this might be more complex than just the punch or withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You think I’m faking it? I’m homeless, I got attacked, and I’m sick. What do you want from me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m not saying you’re faking. But we have to look at all the facts. Your heart is stable. You’re not bleeding. The pain could be from the trauma, or from years of alcohol-related issues—gastritis, nerve pain, muscle strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just give me my meds and let me go. I’ll follow up with cardiology like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed everything. No new heart damage, no infection, no withdrawal complications. We’re ready to discharge you, but we’d like you to stay for one more observation period.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m leaving. I’m tired of being here. I’ll sign out AMA if I have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But please know—your heart meds are critical. Stop drinking, take your Pradaxa, metoprolol, and omeprazole. See cardiology and your doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just need to get out of here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, you’ve left the unit. I’m documenting that you’re leaving against medical advice. Your condition is stable, but the risk of withdrawal seizures and heart issues remains.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard you. I’ll be careful. Just… write down my meds again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll have the nurse give you a list. Please go to the ER or call 911 if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or a seizure. And consider reaching out to social services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, you’re no longer in the hospital. Our records show you left against medical advice early this morning. We hope you stay safe and get the support you need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m gone. Don’t worry about me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do worry. Your health is serious. Please take your medications and avoid alcohol. Your life depends on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented your discharge. You’re responsible for your care now. But we’re here if you come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. Thanks for the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Meléndez. Stay safe out there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This admission is now closed. Patient left against medical advice. Final documentation complete.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Meléndez, I'm Dr. Reyes. You were brought in by EMS after being found unconscious on a bridge. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I... I don’t know. I was drinking. Woke up cold. They gave me something in the ambulance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they gave you Narcan because they thought you might have overdosed. But your blood sugar was low too—60—so you got some fluids and sugar. You’re responding now, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just had a few drinks... maybe more than a few. But I’ve done that before. Why so out of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s a mix of heavy alcohol use and possibly some cocaine in your system. Your labs show acidosis, which means your body is more acidic than it should be—common with intoxication and poor breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cocaine? I used it a while ago, not today. But yeah, I’ve used. My heart’s bad enough as it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know about your heart—dilated cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, and your defibrillator. That’s why we’re watching you closely. But right now, the main issue is the alcohol intoxication and your altered mental state.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better now. Can I go? I don’t like hospitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You were very unresponsive when you arrived. We did a CT scan of your brain and neck to make sure there was no bleeding or fracture. Good news—no injuries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I wasn’t hit. Just passed out. I’ve been sleeping on the street. No home, no meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. And we saw your chest X-ray—no pneumonia or lung issues. But your heart looks enlarged, which we expected. We’re also checking your blood for anemia because you’ve been unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anemia? I feel tired all the time. But it’s hard to eat regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll give you some iron and monitor your levels. But more importantly, we’re worried about alcohol withdrawal. You’ve been admitted before for this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to shake or see bugs again. Last time was bad. But I can’t stay here long—I’ve got nowhere to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on medication to prevent withdrawal—just to keep you safe. You’ll stay overnight so we can monitor you. If you leave now, you could get very sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without withdrawal symptoms. Your breathing’s better, acidosis is improving, and your labs are stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go? I feel okay now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you. But please, try to get back to your cardiologist. Keep your defibrillator checked. And if you want help with alcohol or housing, we can connect you with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thanks for not kicking me out yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take this referral to the shelter clinic. They can help with meds and check your heart. Stay safe, Mr. Meléndez.
